issues.legal_issue: A provision removing limitation for recovery of public-trust property does not revive a property right already extinguished before that provision took effect.
material_facts: The plaintiffs brought a suit to recover property alleged to belong to a public trust under the applicable public-trust legislation.
The disputed properties had been held adversely for long enough that the claims were barred and the property rights extinguished before the limitation-removing provision took effect.
As to one property, the claimant had acquired it by adverse possession before selling it, and it was not identified as trust property when the trust was declared.
issues.conclusion: The limitation-removing provision could not revive property rights already extinguished before it took effect, so the suit remained barred as to the disputed properties. It would override limitation for a claim whose right had not yet been extinguished when the provision took effect.
issues.legal_principle: Section 52A of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, overrides the Limitation Act, 1908, including Section 28, for claims to which it applies, but only where the right to the property had not already been extinguished when Section 52A took effect. Limitation law is procedural, but Section 52A does not restore an extinguished right. The Court approved Mahant Biseshwar Dass v. Sashinath Jhan and Balram Chunnilal v. Durgalal Shivnarain, referred to Mst. Allah Rakhi v. Shah Mohammad Abdur Rahim, and distinguished Dev Chavate v. Ganesh Mahadeo Deshpande.

predicates.public_trust_property_recovery_suit: A claimant brings a proceeding to recover property alleged to belong to a public trust.
predicates.right_extinguished_before_limitation_exc: The property had been possessed adversely for the required period, extinguishing the claimant’s right before a later rule removing the limitation bar took effect.

issues.definition: When a public-trust property recovery suit concerns a right already extinguished before the limitation exception took effect, the exception does not revive the claim.

issues.legal_issue: Expiry of the applicable limitation period during adverse possession extinguishes the former owner's right to the property and gives title to the possessor.
material_facts: The purchasers and their successors possessed the properties adversely from the outset for longer than the applicable limitation period.
The claim to recover the properties became barred well before the recovery suit was brought.
issues.conclusion: Section 28 of the Limitation Act, 1908, extinguished the right to the properties and conferred title by adverse possession on those possessing them.
issues.legal_principle: Section 28 of the Limitation Act, 1908, does more than bar the remedy: once the applicable limitation period expires, it extinguishes the right to the property and the possessor acquires title by adverse possession. The Court did not decide which of Articles 134, 134A, 134B, 142, or 144 applied.

predicates.property_recovery_proceeding: A claimant brings a proceeding seeking recovery of property from a person in possession.
predicates.adverse_possession_for_applicable_limita: The person in possession holds the property adversely for at least the period required to bring a recovery claim.

issues.definition: In a property recovery proceeding, adverse possession lasting for the applicable limitation period results in the possessor acquiring title and the former right being extinguished.
